Australian Broadcasting Corporation (ABC) is Australia's principal public-service broadcaster.

Classical radicalism (from French radical) was a political movement representing the leftward flank of liberalism between the late 18th and early 20th century.

Demosthenes (Attic; 384 - 12 October 322 BC) was a Greek statesman and orator in ancient Athens.

Eleftherios Venizelos was Prime Minister of Greece (1910–20; 1928–33).
Once hailed as "the Desired" and later branded "the Criminal King," this Spanish monarch was overthrown by Napoleon in 1808 before returning to power in 1813 — who was he?
Ferdinand VII (14 October 1784 - 29 September 1833) was King of Spain during the early 19th century.

Born into gentry in Leicestershire, this English courtier caught the eye of King James VI and I at age 21 in 1614, becoming his favourite and 'lover' before being assassinated in the next reign — name this nobleman?
George Villiers, 1st Duke of Buckingham (20 August 1592 - 23 August 1628), was an English courtier, statesman, and notable patron of the arts.
This Karnataka politician, twice chief minister of that state and now a Union minister, is the son of a man who was both Karnataka's chief minister and India's prime minister — who is he?
H. D. Kumaraswamy (born 16 December 1959) is an Indian politician and film producer who is serving as the 21st Minister of Heavy Industries and 14th Minister of Steel of India since 2024.

Hillary Clinton (ne Rodham; born October 26, 1947) is an American politician, lawyer, and diplomat.
Rising through the Tokugawa clan's ranks in the mid-1570s, this Japanese samurai general grew famous after a key battle and is honored as one of the 'Four Guardians' of his shogun — who is he?
Ii Naomasa (March 4, 1561 - March 24, 1602) was a Japanese samurai general and daimyo under the Sengoku period daimy, and later shgun, Tokugawa Ieyasu.

A protégé of Andrew Jackson, this expansionist president saw Texas join the Union, pushed U.S. territory to the Pacific, and settled the Oregon dispute that drew today's U.S.-Canada line — who was he?
James K. Polk (November 2, 1795 - June 15, 1849) was the 11th president of the United States, serving from 1845 to 1849.
The 2004 Democratic presidential nominee, this former Massachusetts senator served as US Secretary of State under Obama and later as the first special envoy for climate — who is he?

John Kerry (born December 11, 1943) is an American attorney, politician, diplomat, and former naval officer who served as the 68th United States secretary of state from 2013 to 2017 in the administration of President Barack Obama.
A member of Germany's parliament since 2005, this physician-turned-politician became a familiar TV face during the COVID-19 pandemic before leading the health ministry from 2021 to 2025 — who is he?
Karl Lauterbach (German; born 21 February 1963) is a German scientist, physician, and politician of the Social Democratic Party (SPD) who served as Federal Minister of Health from 2021 to 2025.
This Indian statesman co-founded a major political party, served as Deputy Prime Minister from 2002 to 2004, and was the longest-serving Home Affairs minister in the country's history. Who is he?
L. K. Advani (born 8 November 1927) is an Indian lawyer, journalist, politician and statesman who served as the 7th Deputy Prime Minister of India from 2002 to 2004.

An Iron Age kingdom in western Anatolia with its capital at Sardis, this state became an Achaemenid satrapy in 546 BC after reaching its greatest extent across western Anatolia the century before — name this kingdom?
Lydia (Ancient) was an Iron Age kingdom situated in western Anatolia, in modern-day Turkey.
This Olympic gold medal-winning equestrian was the first husband of Anne, the Princess Royal, and remains a leading figure in British eventing as a course designer and magazine columnist — who is he?
Mark Phillips (born 22 September 1948) is an English Olympic gold medal-winning horseman who competed for Great Britain.
Which legendary king of Phrygia, son of Gordias and Cybele, is remembered in Greek and Roman mythology for a fabled 'golden touch' that turned everything he handled into pure gold?
Midas (Ancient) was a king of Phrygia with whom many myths became associated, as well as two later members of the Phrygian royal house.

Commonly known by his initials, this Indian politician holds the record for longest-serving chief minister among Telugu states and currently leads Andhra Pradesh as head of the Telugu Desam Party — who is he?
N. Chandrababu Naidu (Telugu; born 20 April 1950), commonly known as CBN, is an Indian politician who is currently serving as the Chief Minister of Andhra Pradesh since 2024.

This former army commander-in-chief seized power in a 2014 coup and went on to serve as Thailand's prime minister until 2023 — who is he?

Prayut Chan-o-cha (born 21 March 1954) is a Thai former politician and military officer who became the 29th prime minister of Thailand after seizing power in the 2014 coup d'tat and served until 2023.

Ibrahim Traoré: Leader of Burkina Faso since 2022.

Italian Social Movement: Neo-fascist political party, 1946–1955.

Lorenzo de' Medici: Lord of Florence from 1469 to 1492.

Mahathir Mohamad: Prime Minister of Malaysia (1981–2003, 2018–2020). Born and raised in Alor Setar, Kedah, Mahathir excelled at school and became a physician.

Dominating the Pontic steppe from the 5th century BC to the 4th century AD, this confederation of ancient Iranian horse nomads formed part of the wider Scythian world — who were they?
Sarmatians: Large Iranian confederation that existed in classical antiquity.

Born in Georgia, this Red Army officer and engineer was the eldest son of a Bolshevik revolutionary who became head of the Soviet Union — who is he?
Yakov Dzhugashvili: Red Army officer and Joseph Stalin's son (1907–1943)
His famous epithet is actually a pun on his name — "noble" plus "counsel" — and this King of the English took the throne after his half-brother Edward the Martyr was assassinated. Who was he?
Æthelred the Unready: King of England (r. 978–1013; 1014–1016)

Zhuge Liang (born 181) is the earliest of the four.
Which one below was born first?
John Ray (born 1627) is the earliest of the four. John Ray (29 November 1627 – 17 January 1705) was an English Christian naturalist and one of the earliest English parson-naturalists.
Fortran (founded 1957) is the earliest of the four.
Which of these came out first?
MUMPS (published 1966) is the earliest of the four.
Pick the physicist from these four.
Laura Bassi is a physicist. Laura Maria Caterina Bassi Veratti (29 October 1711 – 20 February 1778) was an Italian physicist and academic.
Who among these is a chemist?
Carolyn Bertozzi is a chemist. Carolyn Ruth Bertozzi (born October 10, 1966) is an American chemist and Nobel laureate, known for her wide-ranging work spanning both chemistry and biology.
What is the atomic number of Neon?
Neon is a chemical element; it has the symbol Ne and the atomic number 10.
In what year was Kitty Oppenheimer born?
Kitty Oppenheimer: Robert Oppenheimer, the director of the Manhattan Project's Los Alamos Laboratory during World War II.
In what year was Penicillin discovered?
Penicillin was discovered in 1928 by the Scottish physician Alexander Fleming as a crude extract of P. rubens.
In what year was Coulomb's law discovered?
Coulomb's law: This electric force is conventionally called the electrostatic force or Coulomb force.
Which company manufactures Eurocopter AS350 Écureuil?
Eurocopter AS350 Écureuil: Airbus Helicopters. The AS355 Ecureuil 2 is a twin-engine variant, marketed in North America as the TwinStar.
In which country is Gaboon viper?
Gaboon viper: Gabon. It is the largest member of the genus Bitis.
Who is credited with discovering General relativity?
General relativity: Albert Einstein. The relation is specified by the Einstein field equations, a system of second-order partial differential equations.
Who is credited with discovering Tetracycline?
Tetracycline: Lloyd Conover. It is available in oral and topical formulations.
Who is credited with discovering Potassium?
Potassium: Humphry Davy. Potassium is a chemical element; it has symbol K (from Neo-Latin kalium) and atomic number 19.
First added to the DSM in 1980 and diagnosed in women twice as often as men, this condition describes an intense, maladaptive reaction to a stressful life event — what is it?
Adjustment disorder is a mental disorder defined by a maladaptive response to a psychosocial stressor.

Caused by brain damage, disease, or sometimes sedative drugs, this condition splits into a retrograde type that erases memories before an event and an anterograde type that blocks new ones from forming — what is it called?
Amnesia is a deficit in memory caused by brain damage or brain diseases, but it can also be temporarily caused by the use of various sedative and hypnotic drugs.
This severe blood disorder leaves the bone marrow unable to produce enough red cells, white cells, and platelets, often for no known reason — what is it?
Aplastic anemia (AA) is a severe hematologic condition in which the body fails to make blood cells in sufficient numbers.
This fig species develops extra trunks from its own aerial prop roots, letting a single tree spread outward seemingly forever, one variety is even the national tree of India. Name it?
Banyan is a fig that develops accessory trunks from adjacent prop roots, allowing the tree to spread outwards indefinitely.
This colourless industrial compound, easily dissolved in organic solvents but not water, is the key ingredient in most polycarbonate plastics — which chemical?
Bisphenol A (BPA) is a chemical compound primarily used in the manufacturing of various plastics.
Often called a 'chest cold,' this inflammation of the airways in the lungs typically follows an infection that spreads down from the nose or throat. What condition is it?
Bronchitis is inflammation of the bronchi (large and medium-sized airways) in the lungs that causes coughing.
Also called meridian fennel, this biennial plant in the carrot family is native to western Asia, Europe, and North Africa — name it?
Caraway (Carum carvi), also known as meridian fennel, is a biennial plant in the family Apiaceae, native to western Asia, Europe, and North Africa.

Native to North America except for one species found mostly in Asia, these small striped rodents are technically classified as squirrels and pack food into cheek pouches for winter storage — what are they?
Chipmunk are small, striped squirrels of subtribe Tamiina.
Part of the same species as cabbage and broccoli, this loose-leafed member of the 'kale group' has been grown for its big, dark-green leaves since classical antiquity — what is it?
Collard (plant) is a group of loose-leafed cultivars of Brassica oleracea (the same species as many common vegetables, including cabbage and broccoli).
Usually viral and often worse at night, this childhood respiratory infection swells the windpipe to produce a barking, brassy cough and noisy breathing — what's the condition?

Lean, fast, and wedge-skulled, this medium-sized Australian canine comes in ginger, black-and-tan, or creamy white, and scientists still argue whether it's a dog, a wolf subspecies, or its own species — what is it?
Dingo is a lineage of dog found in Australia.
A onetime clerk for Justice Thurgood Marshall, this Harvard Law School dean was tapped for the Supreme Court by President Obama in 2010 — who is she?
Elena Kagan (born April 28, 1960) is an American lawyer who serves as an associate justice of the Supreme Court of the United States.
Known regionally in Shropshire as the 'plum bird,' this small European finch, scientifically Pyrrhula pyrrhula, was the original bird to carry its common English name — which species?
Eurasian bullfinch (Pyrrhula pyrrhula) is a small passerine bird in the finch family, Fringillidae.
Part of the dog family yet famous for a pointed snout and a brush-like tail, the 'true' members of this group belong to the genus Vulpes — what creature is it?
Fox are small-to-medium-sized omnivorous mammals belonging to several genera of the family Canidae.

Built from epithelial tissue with a supporting connective-tissue capsule, this kind of structure secretes hormones straight into the blood if it's ductless, or through a duct to a cavity or surface if not — what is it called?
Gland is a cell or an organ in an animal's body that produces and secretes different substances that the organism needs, either into the bloodstream or into a body cavity or outer surface.
Prehensile and multi-fingered, this appendage sits at the end of primates' forearms, though a few other animals like koalas and raccoons are sometimes described as having one too — which body part?
Hand is a prehensile, multi-fingered appendage located at the end of the forearm or forelimb of primates such as humans, chimpanzees, monkeys, and lemurs.
Originally a variable measure equal to one-twelfth of the night or day in the ancient Near East, this unit of time is now fixed at exactly 3,600 seconds — name this unit?
Hour (symbol: h; also abbreviated hr) is a unit of time historically reckoned as 124 of a day and defined contemporarily as exactly 3,600 seconds.
Once extracted from the leaves of Indigofera plants and now mostly made synthetically, this insoluble blue colorant is famous for dyeing denim and enabling tricks like stone washing. What is it?
Indigo dye is an organic compound with a distinctive blue color.
This American businessman and chemist owned the Los Angeles Lakers through their 'Showtime' era of the 1980s, winning 10 league championships as majority owner. Who is he?
Jerry Buss (January 27, 1933 - February 18, 2013) was an American businessman, investor, chemist, and philanthropist.
Her women's absolute land speed record stood until 2019, she got her own action figure, and Google honored her with a Doodle in 2023 — this deaf stuntwoman and racer. Who is she?
Kitty O'Neil ((1946-03-24)March 24, 1946 - (2018-11-02)November 2, 2018) was an American stuntwoman and auto-racer, often called "the fastest woman in the world" for her various speed records.
Named for the Latin word for weighing scales and lying between Virgo and Scorpius, this faint zodiac constellation has no first-magnitude stars — which one?
Libra (constellation) is a constellation of the zodiac and is located in the Southern celestial hemisphere.

While at IBM in the 1960s, this computer scientist invented a key technique behind the out-of-order execution most modern processors use — then was fired in 1968 for planning a gender transition, an act IBM apologized for in 2020. Who was this engineer?
Lynn Conway (January 2, 1938 - June 9, 2024) was an American computer scientist, electrical engineer, and transgender rights activist.
A German historian, jurist, and political economist born in 1864, he is counted among the central founders of sociology and still shapes social theory today — who was he?

Max Weber (21 April 1864 - 14 June 1920) was a German sociologist, historian, jurist, and political economist who was one of the central figures in the development of sociology and the social sciences more generally.
Also called selective sound sensitivity syndrome, this disorder causes specific everyday sounds to trigger intense, disproportionate emotional and physiological distress — what is it?
Misophonia (or selective sound sensitivity syndrome) is a disorder of decreased tolerance to specific sounds or their associated stimuli, or cues.
Known for strong anabolic but weak androgenic effects, this synthetic androgen is marketed as Deca-Durabolin and used to treat muscle-wasting and bone-density conditions — which steroid?
Nandrolone is an endogenous androgen. Nandrolone esters are used in the treatment of anemias, cachexia (muscle wasting syndrome), osteoporosis, breast cancer, and for other indications.

This biochemical process by which living things use food and water to sustain life can go wrong in either direction, causing malnutrition from either too much or too little of an essential compound — what process is it?
Nutrition is the biochemical and physiological process by which an organism uses food and water to support its life.
This genus of big cats contains the five largest living felines — jaguar, leopard, lion, snow leopard, and tiger — along with extinct relatives like the cave lion — what's the genus called?
Panthera is a genus within the family Felidae, and one of two extant genera in the subfamily Pantherinae.
This flowering plant genus's name traces to a Tupi-Guarani word for tobacco, borrowed via French — which South American garden favorite is it?
Petunia is a genus of 20 species of flowering plants of South American origin.
This inflammation of the lining around the lungs causes sharp chest pain that worsens with breathing, and is most often triggered by a viral infection — what condition is it?
Pleurisy is inflammation of the membranes that surround the lungs and line the chest cavity (pleurae).
Originating in Central Asia despite widespread cultivation elsewhere, this is the most commonly grown species of a fuzzy-skinned stone fruit — what is its scientific name?
Prunus armeniaca is the most commonly cultivated apricot species.

Rooted in Minangkabau cooking, this dish slow-simmers meat in spiced coconut milk until the oil separates and it fries in its own glaze — both a method and a meal across the Malacca Strait; what is it?

Rendang is a fried meat or dry curry made of meat stewed in coconut milk and spices, widely popular across Indonesia, Malaysia, Singapore, Brunei, and the southern parts of the Philippines, where each version is considered local cuisine.
First identified in Wuhan, this positive-sense single-stranded RNA virus prompted the WHO to declare a global health emergency from January 2020 to May 2023 — what's its name?
SARS-CoV-2 (SARSCoV2) is a coronavirus that causes COVID-19, the respiratory illness responsible for the COVID-19 pandemic that began in late 2019.
About 90% of the body's supply of this mood-regulating monoamine is actually made in the gut, where it helps drive intestinal movements — which neurotransmitter is it?
Serotonin (5-HT), is a monoamine neurotransmitter with a wide range of functions in both the central nervous system (CNS) and also peripheral tissues.

This genus of about 60 evergreen flowering plant species, native to the tropical Americas and Southeast Asia, is commonly grown as a houseplant valued for its large leaves and elegant white blooms — what genus is it?
Spathiphyllum is a genus of about 60 species of monocotyledonous flowering plants in the family Araceae, native to tropical regions of the Americas and southeastern Asia.
Educated in Rotterdam through World War II, this Indonesian economist later served as minister of finance, trade, and research under two different presidents — who was he?
Sumitro Djojohadikusumo (27 May 1917 - 9 March 2001) was an Indonesian statesman and one of the country's most influential economists.
Classed among the saurischians and placing them nearer to sauropodomorphs than to ornithischians, these hollow-boned, three-toed dinosaurs were ancestrally meat-eaters — which clade?
Theropoda (from ancient Greek -) is one of the three major clades of dinosaur, alongside Ornithischia and Sauropodomorpha.
Caused by the bacterium Francisella tularensis and treated with the antibiotic streptomycin, this tick-borne illness also goes by an animal-related nickname — what is it?
Tularemia is an infectious disease caused by the bacterium Francisella tularensis.

This forceful expulsion of stomach contents through the mouth can result from food poisoning, pregnancy, motion sickness, or more serious causes like brain tumors, and is usually preceded by nausea — name this bodily reaction?
Vomiting (scientifically known as emesis, and otherwise known as puking, and throwing up) is the forceful expulsion of the contents of one's stomach through the mouth and sometimes the nose.
Each individual's coat is unique, and the best evidence suggests their black-and-white pattern wards off biting flies — which striped African equine is this?
Zebra (subgenus Hippotigris) are African equines with distinctive black-and-white striped coats.
Located behind the nasal cavity where the nose meets the throat, which mass of lymphoid tissue is also known as the pharyngeal tonsil?
Adenoid: Type of tonsil. The adenoid, also known as the pharyngeal tonsil, or nasopharyngeal tonsil is the superior-most of the tonsils.

Born out of wedlock in the Caribbean and orphaned young, this Founding Father became the first U.S. secretary of the treasury and started America's first political party, the Federalist Party — who was he?

Capable of constantly changing its shape by extending and retracting temporary 'false feet,' this single-celled organism turns up across nearly every branch of the eukaryotic tree of life — what is it?
This self-taught Dutch draper turned lensmaker began exploring microbial life with his own single-lensed microscopes in the 1670s, earning him the title 'Father of Microbiology' — who was he?
Writing in 499 CE that he was 23 years old, this pioneering Indian scholar's explicit discussion of the relativity of motion marks him as an early physicist too — who was he?
Squat-bodied and built for digging, this group includes the European, ferret, honey, and American species despite not truly sharing one family tree — what are they?
According to scholar John Carter, this discipline has two senses: a list of works consulted by an author, and the systematic study of books as physical objects — what's it called?
Bibliography: Organized listing of books and the systematic description of them as objects.
Named in allusion to a 'Flying Fortress' that came before it, this pressurized WWII heavy bomber dropped the atomic bombs on Hiroshima and Nagasaki. Which aircraft?
Air warfare of World War II
Boeing B-29 Superfortress: US heavy bomber aircraft, 1942.
Nicknamed 'angel's trumpets' for its pendulous, fragrant blooms, this toxic nightshade-family genus is officially Extinct in the Wild yet thrives worldwide as a garden plant — which genus?
Brugmansia: Genus of flowering plants in the nightshade family.
Which multidrug-resistant fungal yeast colonizes skin in long-term care facilities and causes bloodstream infections with up to a 60% mortality rate?
Also known by the nickname 'catawba,' this genus of flowering trees is native to warm regions of North America, the Caribbean, and East Asia — what genus is it?
Known as lamb's quarters, goosefoot, or fat-hen, this fast-growing annual weed in the amaranth family is sometimes cultivated as food elsewhere — which plant?
Chenopodium album: Species of flowering plant in the goosefoot family.
Native to the Indonesian island that gave part of its scientific name, this legume flower also goes by butterfly pea or blue pea — what is it?

This small, ground-nesting game bird has a call of three quick chirps repeated in succession, breeds across Europe, and winters in Africa and southern India — which species, often confused with a similar-sounding Japanese cousin?
Common quail: Species of bird. The common quail (Coturnix coturnix) or European quail is a small ground-nesting game bird in the pheasant family Phasianidae.
This interdisciplinary field draws on sociology, psychology, and law to study crime, deviant behavior, and the workings of the justice system — what is it called?
Criminology: Field of studies related to crimes.
This Canadian-born entrepreneur co-founded and serves as CEO of Roblox Corporation, after his earlier company was acquired by MSC Software in 1998 — who is he?

Cultivated in China for more than 2,000 years despite not being formally described until 1780, this tree produces the most widely grown fruit in its genus, known by names like Japanese or Chinese persimmon. Which species?
Diospyros kaki: Oriental fruit. Although its first botanical description was not published until 1780, D. kaki cultivation in China dates back more than 2000 years.
Named for its 'skin wings,' this insect order sports pincer-like cerci on its abdomen and displays unusually attentive maternal care for its young — which insect?
Earwig: Order of insects. Damage to foliage, flowers, and various crops is commonly blamed on earwigs, especially the common earwig Forficula auricularia.
Builder of the world's first artificial nuclear reactor, Chicago Pile-1, this Manhattan Project physicist won the 1938 Nobel for work with slow neutrons — who was he?
Grey-buff to pinkish-grey with a black half-collar edged in white, this bird species native to Europe, Asia, and North Africa has also been introduced to Japan and the Americas. What is it?
Eurasian collared dove: Species of bird. The Eurasian collared dove (Streptopelia decaocto), often just collared dove, is a dove species.
First synthesized by Paul Janssen in 1960 and sold under brand names like Duragesic, this synthetic opioid runs 50 to 100 times more potent than morphine — what is it?
Fentanyl: Opioid medication. Fentanyl is a highly potent synthetic opioid of the piperidine family, used primarily as pain medication.
A type of necrotizing tissue infection affecting the genitals or perineum, this condition most often strikes older men, diabetics or the immunocompromised — what is it called?
Fournier gangrene: Medical condition. It most commonly occurs in older men, but it can also occur both in women and children, diabetics, alcoholics, or the immunocompromised.
Also known as the Indian bison, this Vulnerable-listed bovine is the largest living member of the wild cattle family, with most of its roughly 21,000 individuals found in India — what animal is it?
Gaur: Largest species of the bovid family.
Brought to market by Monsanto in 1974 under the brand name Roundup, this herbicide works by blocking a key enzyme that plants need to grow — what is it?
Glyphosate: Systemic herbicide and crop desiccant.
A founder of psychophysics, this German scientist captured how sensation relates to stimulus in a logarithmic law that now bears his and Weber's names — who was he?
Gustav Fechner: German experimental psychologist, physicist, and philosopher (1801–1887)

A pioneer of modern control theory whose collaboration with Claude Shannon helped lay the foundations of the Information Age, he also helped design the automatic guns that defended London from V-1 flying bombs — who was he?
Hendrik Wade Bode: American scientist and engineer (1905–1982)
A pungent root vegetable in the same family as mustard, wasabi, and cabbage, this spice is likely native to Southeastern Europe and Western Asia — what is it?
Horseradish: Species of flowering plants in the cabbage family Brassicaceae.
Native to Southern Europe, the Middle East, and the Caspian region, this mint-family shrub has long been used in traditional herbal medicine as an antiseptic and cough reliever — which plant?

Hyssopus officinalis: Species of plant. Hyssopus officinalis or hyssop is a shrub in the Lamiaceae or mint family native to Southern Europe, the Middle East, and the region surrounding the Caspian Sea.
This condition restricts blood flow to tissue, starving cells of oxygen and nutrients due to causes like thrombosis or embolism — what's it called?
Ischemia: Restriction in blood supply to tissues.
As Grand Pensionary of Holland during the Dutch Golden Age, this statesman dominated politics from 1650 until the 'Disaster Year' of 1672 — who was he?

A NASA mathematician and human computer, she calculated the orbital mechanics critical to America's first crewed spaceflights and was among the first African-American women to work as a NASA scientist — who was she?
Native to the Mediterranean and used to season food as a bay leaf, this aromatic evergreen prominent in classical Greco-Roman culture can grow up to 20 metres tall — what is its scientific name?
Laurus nobilis: Species of flowering plant in the laurel family Lauraceae.
Soft, movable, and painless, this benign fatty-tissue growth most often shows up under the skin on the upper back, shoulders, or abdomen — what is it?
Lipoma: Benign tumor made of fat tissue.
This common, nonspecific medical sign involves lymph nodes becoming abnormally swollen or enlarged, with causes ranging from the common cold to cancer. What's the condition called?
Lymphadenopathy: Abnormal change in size of the lymph nodes.
A student of Marie Curie, this French physicist discovered the element francium in 1939 and later became the first woman elected to the French Académie des Sciences — who was she?

Encompassing conditions marked by a clinically significant disturbance in thinking, emotional regulation, or behavior that causes real distress or impaired functioning, this broad psychiatric category has causes that remain often unclear — what is the umbrella term for it?

Given the NATO reporting name 'Hip,' this Soviet-designed helicopter family has been in continuous production since 1975 as a medium twin-turbine transport, with an armed gunship variant — which aircraft?
Mil Mi-17: Family of Russian military transport helicopters.
Forming dense green mats with leaves just one cell thick, these seedless plants reproduce via spore-topped stalks called sporophytes — which plants?
Moss: Division of typically non-vascular land plants.
The sole surviving family of an ancient cephalopod lineage, these nine living species carry coiled chambered shells 10 to 25 cm across and are all protected under CITES — what creatures are they?
Nautilus: Family of molluscs. It comprises nine living species in two genera, the type of which is the genus Nautilus.

As the United States' first swept-wing fighter jet, this Korean War-era aircraft dueled Soviet MiG-15s in some of history's earliest jet-to-jet battles — which plane, produced in more than 7,800 units?
North American F-86 Sabre: Family of US fighter aircraft.
The most arboreal of the great apes, with long arms, short legs and reddish-brown hair, this genus Pongo primate survives today only in the rainforests of Borneo and Sumatra — what is it?
Orangutan: Genus of Asian apes. The most arboreal of the great apes, orangutans spend most of their time in trees.

Named for its resemblance to a related crested dinosaur, this duck-billed herbivore could grow over 9 meters long, moved on two or four legs, and was first described in 1922 by William Parks — which dinosaur genus?
Parasaurolophus: Hadrosaurid ornithopod dinosaur genus from Late Cretaceous Period.
Created by Larry Wall in 1987 as a Unix scripting tool for report processing, this language's planned sixth version was eventually spun off and renamed Raku — which programming language?
Perl: Interpreted programming language first released in 1987.
Manufactured in Switzerland since 1991, this pressurized single-engine turboprop's large aft cargo door has made it popular with air-ambulance operators and police departments alike — which aircraft?
Pilatus PC-12: Swiss executive and utility transport aircraft.
Emerging in the 1960s as scholars from once-colonized nations began writing back, this academic field examines the lingering cultural and political effects of empire — what's it called?
Postcolonialism: Study of the cultural legacy of colonialism and imperialism.
This emotional response to severe distressing events like violence or a life-threatening injury can trigger flashbacks, panic attacks, insomnia, and post-traumatic stress disorder — what's it called?
Psychological trauma: Emotional response caused by severe distressing events.
This genus of roughly 1,750 flowering plant species includes the buttercups, spearworts, and water crowfoots — which genus?
Ranunculus: Genus of flowering plants in the buttercup family.
Its seeds yield castor oil but also harbor a highly potent toxin — which plant genus, better known for producing the castor bean?
Ricinus: Monotypic genus of plant in the spurge family.
Sold under the brand name Ventolin, this fast-acting inhaled medication opens the airways within about 15 minutes to treat asthma attacks and COPD — what is it?
Salbutamol: Short-acting bronchodilator used for acute asthma.
This long-term skin condition causes flaky, greasy patches on the scalp, face, and chest, and is called cradle cap when it appears on a baby's scalp — what is it?
Seborrhoeic dermatitis: Skin disease. Seborrhoeic dermatitis (also spelled seborrheic dermatitis in American English) is a long-term skin disorder.
The brightest star in Earth's night sky, this binary system in Canis Major pairs a bright main-sequence star with a faint white dwarf companion — which star?
Sirius: Brightest star in Earth's night sky. Its name is derived from the Greek word Σείριος (Latin script: Seirios; lit. 'glowing' or 'scorching').

Made of a segmented series of bones cushioned by intervertebral discs, this defining feature of some 50,000 animal species surrounds and protects the nerve tissue running through it — what is it, also known as the backbone?
Spinal column: Bony structure found in vertebrates.

This small nocturnal marsupial has membranes stretching from its forelegs to hindlegs that let it soar between trees, and its scientific name translates to 'short-headed rope-dancer' — what animal is it?
Sugar glider: Species of Australian marsupial.
A staple from the Caribbean to Oceania to East Asia, this Araceae-family plant is prized for the starchy underground corm it grows much like a yam — what is it?
Taro: Species of plant. Taro (Colocasia esculenta) is a root vegetable.
After dropping out of Stuyvesant High School and serving in the Korean War, this economist went on to earn a PhD from Chicago and a National Humanities Medal in 2002?
Co-founder and former CEO of a ride-hailing giant, this businessman resigned in 2017 amid allegations he ignored harassment reports, later selling most of his shares for $2.5 billion — who is he?
Travis Kalanick: American entrepreneur and former CEO of Uber.
This medical condition occurs when kidney failure allows urea and other metabolic waste products to build up dangerously in the bloodstream. What's it called?
Uremia: Excess urea in the blood due to kidney dysfunction.
Known as the 'true foxes,' animals in this genus are smaller and bushier-tailed than any wolf or jackal, with a signature dark triangular mask between the eyes — which genus?
Vulpes: Genus of true foxes. The members of this genus are colloquially referred to as true foxes, meaning they form a proper clade.

A physician by training, this Polish politician has served as Deputy Prime Minister and Minister of National Defence since 2023, after leading his country's labour ministry a decade earlier — who is he?
Władysław Kosiniak-Kamysz: Polish physician and politician (born 1981)
